title: Co-Evolving Harnesses and Models: On-Policy Correction Helps Weaker Models Catch Up Where Imitation Fails

numericClaims.quote: Consistent with prior reports, evolving the harness lifts task success: mean test success rises from 29.2% under the base harness to 78.0% under the evolved harness (Table 1, rows 1–2), a gain of 48.8 points that holds across tasks.

We evolve this harness using only the weaker Qwen model, yet the stronger expert gemini-3.1-pro-preview operates it just as well: the expert improves from 84.4% under the base harness to 93.6% under the evolved harness (Table 1, rows 3–4, +9.2 on average).

Surprisingly, this recipe lowers Qwen’s mean test success from 78.0% to 63.1% (Table 1, rows 2 and 5), and the regression holds across all seven tasks, ranging from −4.2 points on anomaly detection to −29.9 on payroll auditing (−14.9 on average).
The evolved harness lifts the weak Gemma from 46.7% to 55.6% (+8.9).

To the contrary, the model still exercises the harness’s task-specific components: it triggers almost every harness edit in its rollouts, and it actually raises its use of the domain-computation recipe from 30.8% to 76.1% (Table 2).
What breaks instead is planning: planning failures emerge as an essentially new failure mode, rising from 1.1% to 14.6% of failures (+13.5).

it raises mean test success from 78.0% to 79.7% (+1.7), gaining on five of seven tasks—website management (+5.6), stock alerting (+2.2), code refactoring (+2.2), anomaly detection (+1.7), and browser automation (+1.2)—and staying within noise on the two tasks where the harness has likely already saturated (budget approval −0.6, payroll auditing −0.4).

We run each task under three random seeds with a budget of $20 and a 600 s per-rollout time limit, and select the best harness h∗ as the candidate with the highest validation score (ties broken by the earliest iteration).
We sample N = 3 candidate corrections per turn and keep the best one under a quality judge.

questions.question: What two levers for adapting an agent to a domain does the paper study, and which lightweight method represents the model lever?
questions.answer: Harness evolution (editing the system prompt, tool set, execution hooks, and context-management scaffolding) and model-weight adaptation, represented by parameter-efficient fine-tuning such as LoRA-SFT.

questions.question: What happens when the weaker Qwen model is fine-tuned on the expert's trajectories under the evolved harness versus under the baseline harness?
questions.answer: Under the evolved harness, imitation lowers mean test success from 78.0% to 63.1%, regressing on all seven tasks (−14.9 on average, from −4.2 on anomaly detection to −29.9 on payroll auditing); the identical recipe under the unevolved baseline harness helps, raising success from 29.2% to 35.5% (+6.3).

questions.question: How well does the harness evolved for the weaker model transfer upward to the stronger expert?
questions.answer: The expert gemini-3.1-pro-preview improves from 84.4% under the base harness to 93.6% under the evolved harness (+9.2 on average), triggers nearly every evolved edit in 93.6–100% of its rollouts, and uses the domain-computation recipe in 94.2% of rollouts (vs 30.8% for the base model).

questions.question: What is the paper's diagnosis of why expert imitation fails under the evolved harness?
questions.answer: Planning-strategy drift: the weaker model adopts the expert's planning strategy without the competence to execute it and no longer fits a harness evolved around its native planning style. Knowledge and scaffold usage actually increase (domain-computation recipe use rises from 30.8% to 76.1%), but planning failures rise from 1.1% to 14.6% of failures (+13.5).

questions.question: How does the on-policy expert-correction pipeline work?
questions.answer: A self-directed meta-level MLE agent localizes the single failing turn in each of the weaker model's own rollouts under the evolved harness; the expert model rewrites only that one turn in place (N = 3 candidate corrections sampled per turn, best kept under a quality judge); the weaker model is then LoRA-SFT'd on these minimally edited trajectories (~500 rows: ~400 in-place expert corrections plus ~50 self-pass rows), preserving its planning distribution.

questions.question: What gain does on-policy correction deliver over the evolved-harness baseline, and on which tasks?
questions.answer: Mean test success rises from 78.0% to 79.7% (+1.7), gaining on five of seven tasks—website management (+5.6), stock alerting (+2.2), code refactoring (+2.2), anomaly detection (+1.7), browser automation (+1.2)—and staying within noise on budget approval (−0.6) and payroll auditing (−0.4).

questions.question: What does the Gemma replication on the Webarena task show?
questions.answer: The evolved harness lifts weak Gemma from 46.7% to 55.6% (+8.9) and the expert from 71.1% to 81.1% (+10.0), yet fine-tuning Gemma on the expert's trajectories regresses it to 41.1%—14.5 points below its evolved-harness baseline and 5.6 points below even its default-harness baseline—showing the regression is not specific to the Qwen–Gemini pairing.

questions.question: Which models serve as the weaker students and which as the expert/reflection models?
questions.answer: Students: qwen3-coder-30b-a3b-instruct (30B total / 3B active) and gemma-4-26b-a4b-it (26B/4B active); expert and GEPA-style reflection/meta-agent: gemini-3.1-pro-preview.

questions.question: What LoRA fine-tuning configuration is used?
questions.answer: LoRA rank 16 or 64 (best scores reported), 2 epochs, learning rate 1e−4, bf16, effective batch size 8, sequence length 49,152 tokens (plus 98,304-token context if >5% of training data suffers truncation); adapters merged into a dense checkpoint served with tensor parallelism across two H200 GPUs; a single run completes in under an hour.

questions.question: What are the seven enterprise agentic tasks in the benchmark suite?
questions.answer: Payroll (attendance) auditing, budget approval, stock alerting, IoT anomaly detection, browser automation (Playwright), website management, and code refactoring.
